title: How to Get More Interviews (Without Sounding Like Everyone Else)
description:
If your resume sounds like everyone else's, recruiters may reject it before they ever read your experience.

In this video, I'll show you the wording shifts that make qualified professionals sound more strategic, more credible, and more interview-worthy—without lying, exaggerating, or stuffing your resume with buzzwords.

You'll learn:
 Why recruiters judge your level in seconds
 The biggest professional summary mistakes
 How to sound more senior using the experience you already have
 The language that makes recruiters keep reading
 Real before-and-after resume examples

transcript: You're probably getting rejected before recruiters even read your experience. [music] Not because you're unqualified, but because your resume sounds less experience than you [music] actually are. Recruiters can usually tell who sounds senior, strategic, and leadership level within [music] seconds of scanning a resume. And two people can have almost identical backgrounds. Well, one sounds highly valuable and worth interviewing, [music] and the other sounds junior without even realizing it. Most of the time that [music] difference comes down to language. In this video, I'm going to show you exactly [music] how recruiters judge your level leadership and value using your professional summary. And I'm going to break down the exact wording shifts that instantly make you sound more credible, more strategic, and more interview-worthy without lying or stuffing your resume with buzzwords. Because recruiters are not just reading your resume, they're sizing you up and deciding if you're a fit for their role. Hi, if we haven't met yet, I'm Kate Courseler, your career strategist and your career bestie. I help qualified professionals stop getting overlooked and start positioning themselves like the obvious choice. Let's get right into it. One of the biggest mistakes people make with professional summaries is that they write them like biographies. They write long introductions, generic descriptions, responsibilities, and buzzwords that honestly sound exactly like everyone else. You have probably seen summaries just like this before. Dedicated professional experience in collaborating with teams and supporting organizational goals. But what does that actually even mean? Seriously, everybody says they are dedicated. Recruiters are not looking for generic descriptions, they are looking for signals. Signals of leadership, signals of scope, signals of confidence, and signals of business impact. They are looking for signals that instantly tell them this person operates at a higher level, and they decide that fast. Your professional summary is not there to explain your life story. It is there to position you. Before recruiters even hit your experience section, your summary has already told them whether you sound strategic or task-focused, leadership-oriented or support level, confident or vague, like someone who owns outcomes or someone who just participated in them. That framing changes everything. Let me show you exactly what I mean. Here's how weaker summaries usually sound. Dedicated mental health professional with experience providing counseling services, managing caseloads, collaborating with teams, and supporting client needs. Now, technically, is that wrong? No, but it sounds small. It sounds task-focused, and honestly, it sounds like thousands of other resumes for people in the mental health field that recruiters looked at that week. Now, listen to this version instead. Licensed professional counselor and certified rehabilitation counselor with experience supervising vocational and mental health programs serving individuals with disabilities, including severe and persistent mental illness, substance use disorders, veterans, and justice-involved populations. Strategic leader with a proven track record of guiding teams of up to 25 staff, scaling programs to double in size, and driving outcomes including a 95% job retention and reduced recidivism. Skilled in implementing evidence-based practices and securing over 750,000 in funding to support program growth and performance. Hear the difference? The second version sounds more strategic, more credible, more leadership-focused, and much more valuable. And the reason why is because a strong summary establishes level immediately. If you lead people, say it. If you own programs, say it. If you manage operations, funding system, outcomes, growth, performance, say it. Recruiters are constantly scanning for indicators of complexity and scope because that is what signals seniority. Watch how wording alone changes perception. A weaker version might say, "Work with leadership teams to support initiatives across multiple locations." But a stronger version sounds like this, "Partnered with executive leadership across 12 locations to improve operational performance, streamline workflows, and reduce reporting delays by 35%." Those are two completely different perceived levels even though they are describing very similar work. Here's another example. A weak version might say, "Help clients with employment goals and job placement support." But a stronger version sounds like this, "Improved employment outcomes for individuals with significant barriers to employment contributing to a 95% job retention rate and increase program placement success across multiple community partnerships." Again, one sounds like participation while the other sounds like ownership and measurable impact. And that difference matters way more than most people realize. Strong summaries focus on impact, not responsibilities. Weak summaries talk about tasks while strong summaries talk about outcomes like growth, retention, funding, revenue, scaling, leadership, performance improvement. That is what makes somebody sound senior. Specificity matters a lot here, too, because generic language weakens credibility almost instantly while specific language creates authority. "Helped clients" sounds vague, but "achieved 95% job retention and secured over 750,000 in funding" sounds measurable, strategic, and real. Specificity builds trust fast. And another huge difference is that strong summaries connect directly to the problem the role is designed to solve. Every single job exists because something needs to grow, improve, stabilize, scale, organize, lead, or just get fixed. Your summary should immediately communicate, "I'm solving this type of problem." Because that's what the recruiters are actually trying to figure out during a quick resume scan. This is also why two people with similar experience can get completely different results. One sounds like they participated, while the other sounds like they led. One sounds reactive, while the other sounds strategic. One sounds replaceable, while the other sounds invaluable. Now, let's talk about one of the fastest ways people accidentally weaken their resume without realizing it. Passive language. Words like assisted with, helped, responsible for, and worked on instantly shrink your perceived impact. Stronger candidates sound ownership oriented. They say things like led, implemented, directed, launched, scaled, developed, and improved. For example, a weaker bullet might say, "Responsible for overseeing staff and supporting daily operations." But a stronger version sounds like this, "Led a team of 25 staff across vocational and mental health programs, improving retention outcomes and supporting program expansion that doubled service capacity." Or instead of saying, "Worked on process improvements," a stronger version would sound like this. "Implemented workflow improvements that reduced reporting delays by 35% and improved operational efficiency across multi-site programs." That language changes perceptions fast. And perception is everything during a quick resume scan. Recruiters are not carefully studying every single word on your resume. They are rapidly gathering signals about who feels capable, strategic, credible, and worth interviewing. If your summary sounds weak, the rest of your resume has to work 10 times harder to recover from that first impression. But when your summary immediately positions you as strategic, [music] relevant, and high-value, recruiters start reading the rest of your resume looking for reasons to move you forward. That creates a completely different [music] psychological experience.
